title: Networking & Protocols
summary: Every service you deploy communicates over a network. Understanding the OSI model, TCP/IP, HTTP, and DNS is not theoretical — it directly determines how you debug connection failures, design service meshes, and secure traffic.

sections.title: The OSI model and TCP/IP in practice
sections.body:
The **OSI model** (Open Systems Interconnection) is the foundational framework for understanding how computers communicate over a network. It divides the problem of networked communication into seven distinct layers, each with a clear responsibility. While engineers rarely talk about layer 2 or layer 5 in daily conversation, the model gives you precise vocabulary for diagnosing problems: a "layer 3 issue" means routing, a "layer 7 issue" means the application protocol.

In practice, the OSI model maps closely onto the **TCP/IP protocol suite** that actually runs the internet. TCP/IP compresses the seven OSI layers into four: Network Access (OSI 1–2), Internet (OSI 3), Transport (OSI 4), and Application (OSI 5–7). When you run `curl https://api.example.com`, every layer in that stack is active simultaneously — DNS uses UDP at layer 4, TCP connects at layer 4, TLS negotiates at layer 6, and HTTP exchanges data at layer 7.

**Why this matters for DevOps:** when something is broken, the layer tells you what to check. A connection timeout at layer 4 means the TCP three-way handshake never completed — check firewall rules, security groups, or whether a process is listening. A 502 Bad Gateway at layer 7 means TCP connected fine but the application response was invalid — check the backend process, not the network. Distinguishing these saves hours of debugging.

**TCP vs UDP** is the most consequential choice at layer 4. TCP's three-way handshake (`SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK`) guarantees that both sides are ready before any data flows, and the protocol retransmits lost packets automatically. This reliability has a cost: latency and CPU overhead. UDP skips the handshake entirely — packets are sent without acknowledgment, which makes it ideal for real-time traffic (video, DNS, gaming) where a retransmit would arrive too late to be useful anyway.

**Port numbers** at layer 4 act like apartment numbers in a building: the IP address gets packets to the right host; the port routes them to the right application. A process registers itself with the OS by calling `bind()` on a port. If nothing is listening on port 8080, a connection attempt gets an immediate `Connection refused` (a TCP RST packet). If a firewall silently drops packets instead, you get a timeout — that distinction alone tells you whether the problem is "nothing listening" or "blocked before it arrives."

```
Layer 7 — Application   HTTP, HTTPS, DNS, SSH, SMTP, gRPC
Layer 6 — Presentation  TLS/SSL encryption, encoding
Layer 5 — Session       Connection management, sessions
Layer 4 — Transport     TCP (reliable), UDP (fast)
Layer 3 — Network       IP addressing, routing
Layer 2 — Data Link     MAC addresses, Ethernet, ARP
Layer 1 — Physical      Cables, radio signals
```

**Where you spend your time:**
- **L7**: HTTP status codes, headers, timeouts, TLS certificates
- **L4**: TCP connection refused vs timeout (is the port open? is the process listening?)
- **L3**: Routing issues, VPC subnets, security group rules

**TCP vs UDP:**

```
TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)
  ✓ Reliable — guarantees delivery, retransmits lost packets
  ✓ Ordered — packets arrive in order
  ✓ Connection-oriented — 3-way handshake (SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK)
  ✗ Higher overhead
  Used for: HTTP/S, SSH, database connections

UDP (User Datagram Protocol)
  ✓ Fast — no connection overhead, no retransmit
  ✗ Unreliable — packets may drop or arrive out of order
  Used for: DNS queries, video streaming, game traffic
```

**Ports you must know:**

```
22    SSH
53    DNS (UDP/TCP)
80    HTTP
443   HTTPS
3306  MySQL
5432  PostgreSQL
6379  Redis
6443  Kubernetes API server
8080  Common dev/alt HTTP
```

```bash
# Check if a port is open on a remote host
# Test against the k3s API server (always present in the sandbox)
nc -zv k3s 6443

# See what's listening locally
ss -tlnp
```

sections.title: HTTP and HTTPS: how the web actually works
sections.body:
**HTTP** (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) is the language that web clients and servers use to exchange resources. Every REST API call, webhook delivery, Kubernetes API request, health check, and browser page load is an HTTP transaction. Despite being invisible to end users, HTTP is arguably the most important protocol for a DevOps engineer to understand deeply.

HTTP is a **stateless, text-based, request–response protocol**. Stateless means the server remembers nothing between requests — each request must carry all the context it needs (authentication tokens, session IDs, and so on). Text-based means you can read and construct messages by hand, which is why `curl` and `openssl s_client` are such powerful debugging tools.

**HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3:** HTTP/1.1 opens a new TCP connection per request by default (or reuses one with `Connection: keep-alive`). HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests over a single TCP connection using binary framing — the Kubernetes API server and gRPC both use HTTP/2. HTTP/3 replaces TCP with QUIC (a UDP-based transport), reducing latency on lossy connections.

**Headers** carry metadata about the request or response. The `Host` header tells the server which virtual host is being requested — critical for reverse proxies serving multiple domains from one IP. `Content-Type` tells the receiver how to parse the body (JSON, form data, binary). `Authorization` carries credentials. `X-Forwarded-For` carries the original client IP when a proxy is in the path — if your application logs show every request coming from `10.0.0.1` (the nginx IP), you need this header propagated from your proxy config.

**Status codes** are a structured vocabulary for outcomes. The hundred-series groupings are load-bearing: 2xx means success, 4xx means the client did something wrong, 5xx means the server failed. Distinguishing a 401 (not authenticated — credentials missing or invalid) from a 403 (authenticated but not authorized — wrong permissions) immediately directs you toward the right fix. A 502 Bad Gateway from nginx means nginx couldn't get a valid response from the upstream — the backend is probably down or crashing. A 504 Gateway Timeout means the backend is alive but responding too slowly.

HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) is the protocol powering every REST API, web app, and webhook you'll work with.

**Request structure:**
```
GET /api/pods?namespace=default HTTP/1.1
Host: k8s-api.example.com
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGci...
Content-Type: application/json
Accept: application/json
```

**Response structure:**
```
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
X-Request-Id: abc-123

{"items": [...]}
```

**HTTP methods:**
```
GET     — read a resource (idempotent, no side effects)
POST    — create a resource
PUT     — replace a resource entirely
PATCH   — update part of a resource
DELETE  — delete a resource
HEAD    — like GET but no body (check if resource exists)
```

**Status codes:**
```
2xx — Success
  200 OK           — request succeeded
  201 Created      — resource was created
  204 No Content   — success, no body

3xx — Redirect
  301 Moved Permanently
  302 Found (temporary redirect)

4xx — Client error
  400 Bad Request  — malformed input
  401 Unauthorized — missing/invalid authentication
  403 Forbidden    — authenticated but not authorized
  404 Not Found    — resource doesn't exist
  409 Conflict     — state conflict (e.g. already exists)
  422 Unprocessable Entity — validation failed
  429 Too Many Requests — rate limited

5xx — Server error
  500 Internal Server Error — bug in the server
  502 Bad Gateway           — upstream server returned invalid response
  503 Service Unavailable   — service down or overloaded
  504 Gateway Timeout       — upstream didn't respond in time
```

```bash
# Inspect HTTP responses
curl -I https://kubernetes.io/docs/   # headers only
curl -v https://httpbin.org/get       # verbose: full exchange
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://example.com  # just status

# Follow redirects (-L), ignore TLS errors (-k), set timeout
curl -Lk --max-time 10 http://service.local/health
```

sections.title: DNS: the internet's phonebook
sections.body:
**DNS** (Domain Name System) is the distributed database that translates human-readable hostnames into IP addresses. It is one of the most critical and most misunderstood systems in the internet stack. Virtually every network operation begins with a DNS lookup, and DNS failures are responsible for a disproportionate share of "the site is down" incidents — even when the site itself is perfectly healthy.

DNS works as a **hierarchical, delegated tree**. The root of the tree is `.` (the root zone), served by a small set of globally distributed root nameservers. Below that come **top-level domains** like `.com`, `.io`, `.org`, each managed by a registry. Below those are **second-level domains** like `example.com`, where you register and control your own authoritative nameservers. This hierarchy is why DNS is both robust (no single point of failure) and occasionally slow (a fresh lookup can require querying three or four servers in sequence).

**Caching** is central to DNS performance and a frequent source of confusion. Every DNS response includes a **TTL** (time-to-live) in seconds, instructing resolvers how long to cache the answer. A TTL of 300 means the IP may be stale for up to five minutes after you update it. This is why DNS changes "take time to propagate" — each caching layer (your OS resolver, your ISP's resolver, corporate DNS) holds an old answer until its TTL expires. Before a major migration, lower your TTLs days in advance so you can change IPs quickly when the moment comes.

**DNS record types** map to specific use cases. `A` and `AAAA` records map names to IPv4 and IPv6 addresses. `CNAME` creates an alias from one name to another — useful for CDNs and service aliases, but a CNAME cannot be placed at the zone apex (`example.com` itself must use an A record). `MX` records tell mail servers where to deliver email for a domain. `TXT` records store arbitrary text and are used for domain ownership verification (Google, Let's Encrypt), SPF/DKIM anti-spoofing, and more. `SRV` records encode a hostname, port, and weight — Kubernetes uses them internally for service discovery.

**Kubernetes DNS** runs an in-cluster resolver called **CoreDNS**. Every pod's `/etc/resolv.conf` points to the CoreDNS ClusterIP as its nameserver. When a pod in the `default` namespace queries `my-service`, CoreDNS expands it through a search path to `my-service.default.svc.cluster.local` and returns the Service's ClusterIP. Understanding this expansion explains why cross-namespace calls need the full `service.namespace` format, and why a typo in a namespace name produces a silent DNS failure rather than a clear error message.

DNS (Domain Name System) translates human-readable names to IP addresses. Most connectivity issues in distributed systems come down to DNS.

**How DNS resolution works:**

```
browser asks: "what is the IP for api.example.com?"

1. Check /etc/hosts (local override)
2. Check local DNS cache
3. Query DNS resolver (configured in /etc/resolv.conf)
4. Resolver checks cache — if not found:
5. Resolver queries root nameservers (.) → which TLD server handles .com?
6. Queries .com TLD nameservers → which NS handles example.com?
7. Queries example.com nameservers → what is api.example.com?
8. Returns A record (IPv4) or AAAA record (IPv6)
```

**DNS record types:**
```
A        maps hostname to IPv4 address
AAAA     maps hostname to IPv6 address
CNAME    alias from one hostname to another
MX       mail server for a domain
TXT      arbitrary text (used for SPF, DMARC, verification)
NS       nameservers for a domain
SRV      service location record (used by Kubernetes)
PTR      reverse DNS (IP → hostname)
```

```bash
# Query DNS
dig google.com                     # full response
dig google.com A                   # just A records
dig google.com MX                  # mail records
dig +short google.com              # just the IP
dig @8.8.8.8 google.com            # query specific resolver (8.8.8.8 = Google)

# Trace the full resolution chain
dig +trace google.com

# Reverse lookup (IP → hostname)
dig -x 8.8.8.8

# Check DNS in Kubernetes
# CoreDNS runs inside the cluster and resolves service names
# Service DNS format: <service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local
COREDNS=$(kubectl get svc kube-dns -n kube-system -o jsonpath='{.spec.clusterIP}')
dig @$COREDNS argocd-server.argocd.svc.cluster.local

# /etc/resolv.conf defines where to send DNS queries
cat /etc/resolv.conf

# /etc/hosts takes priority over DNS
cat /etc/hosts
```

**Kubernetes DNS pattern:**
```
Service name:       web-app
Full DNS name:      web-app.default.svc.cluster.local
From same ns:       web-app
From other ns:      web-app.default
Cross-cluster:      web-app.default.svc.cluster.local
```

sections.title: Firewalls, security groups, and network policies
sections.body:
**Firewalls** are access control systems that inspect network packets and decide whether to allow or deny them. Every host in a production environment has firewall rules operating at multiple layers simultaneously: on the Linux host itself (via iptables or nftables), at the cloud provider level (security groups, network ACLs), and within Kubernetes (Network Policies). Understanding all three levels is essential both for securing infrastructure and for diagnosing "connection refused" or "connection timed out" errors efficiently.

**iptables** is the Linux kernel's built-in packet filtering framework, and it is far more pervasive than most engineers realize. Rules are organized into chains (`INPUT`, `OUTPUT`, `FORWARD`) within tables (`filter`, `nat`, `mangle`). The kernel evaluates rules top-to-bottom and stops at the first match. This ordering matters critically: a DROP rule placed before an ACCEPT rule silently blocks traffic. Importantly, Docker itself manages iptables — when you run `docker run -p 8080:80`, Docker automatically inserts a DNAT rule in the `nat` table to redirect host port 8080 to the container's port 80. Understanding this prevents confusion when you see rules you didn't write and explains why Docker port publishing works even without explicit firewall configuration.

**Cloud security groups** (AWS) and firewall rules (GCP) work differently from raw iptables because they are **stateful**. Stateful means that if an outbound connection is allowed, the return traffic is automatically permitted regardless of inbound rules — the firewall tracks connection state. This statefulness prevents a classic mistake where engineers allow outbound traffic but forget inbound return packets. Security groups in AWS attach to network interfaces (ENIs), and a single instance can have multiple groups whose rules are unioned together (most permissive wins).

**Kubernetes Network Policies** operate at the pod level using label selectors rather than IP addresses. By default, Kubernetes allows unrestricted pod-to-pod communication — any pod can reach any other pod on any port in the cluster. Network Policies introduce selective isolation: once you apply *any* Network Policy that selects a pod, that pod begins rejecting all traffic not explicitly allowed by a matching policy. This default-deny-on-selection behavior is the most common source of confusion: adding a Network Policy to restrict one type of traffic can silently break other traffic to the same pod if that other traffic isn't explicitly allowed.

**Diagnosing firewall issues:** the error message tells you which layer to investigate. `Connection refused` means the packet arrived at the host but nothing was listening (or the host sent a TCP RST). `Connection timed out` means the packet never arrived — a firewall or router is silently dropping it. `No route to host` means the kernel couldn't find a path at all (routing table issue). These three outcomes map directly to different debugging strategies and dramatically narrow your search.

A firewall controls which traffic is allowed to reach a network or host. In cloud environments, this is usually called a 'security group' or 'network ACL'.

```bash
# ── iptables (Linux firewall) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# View current rules
iptables -L -n -v

# Allow incoming SSH
iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT

# Allow incoming HTTP/S
iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 80 -j ACCEPT
iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 443 -j ACCEPT

# Drop everything else incoming
iptables -A INPUT -j DROP

# ── ufw (Uncomplicated Firewall — Ubuntu wrapper around iptables) ─────────
ufw status
ufw allow 22/tcp
ufw allow 80/tcp
ufw allow from 10.0.0.0/8 to any port 5432  # only internal IPs to postgres
ufw enable

# ── AWS Security Groups ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Security groups are stateful: if you allow outbound, inbound response is auto-allowed
# Common mistake: allowing 0.0.0.0/0 on port 22 (should use VPN or bastion)

# ── Kubernetes Network Policies ──────────────────────────────────────────
# By default, all pods can talk to all other pods
# Network Policies restrict traffic at the pod level
```

```yaml
# Allow only traffic from pods with label app=frontend to app=backend
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-frontend-to-backend
  namespace: default
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: backend
  ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: frontend
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 8080
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
```

```bash
# In the sandbox: apply and inspect network policies
kubectl get networkpolicies -A

# Test connectivity using a real pod in the sandbox
kubectl exec deploy/argocd-server -n argocd -- wget -qO- http://localhost:8080/healthz
```

sections.title: Exercise: network debugging in the sandbox
sections.body:
Network debugging is a systematic skill. Rather than guessing, experienced engineers work through a mental checklist: Can I resolve the name? Can I reach the IP? Is the port open? Is the application responding? Does the HTTP response make sense? This exercise walks you through each layer of that diagnostic process on the live sandbox cluster.

The sandbox runs a real k3s Kubernetes cluster inside Docker. This means you have multiple layers of networking active simultaneously: the host Docker bridge network, the k3s CNI overlay network (Flannel by default), Kubernetes Service ClusterIPs, and CoreDNS for in-cluster name resolution. Tracing a request from your terminal to a pod response crosses all of these layers, which makes the sandbox an ideal environment to practice systematic network debugging.

As you run these commands, pay attention to what each tool tests. `nc -zv` tests layer 4 (TCP connectivity). `dig` tests DNS resolution. `curl -v` tests layer 7 (HTTP response and TLS). `ss -tlnp` reveals which processes are bound to which ports. Together they give you a complete picture of the network stack between two endpoints.

```bash
# 1. DNS resolution inside the cluster
# Find the CoreDNS service IP
kubectl get svc kube-dns -n kube-system

# Query it to resolve service names
kubectl run -it --rm dns-test --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -- \
  nslookup argocd-server.argocd.svc.cluster.local

# 2. Inspect pod networking
kubectl get pods -A -o wide    # shows IP of each pod

# 3. Check what ports the ArgoCD server is listening on
kubectl exec -n argocd deploy/argocd-server -- ss -tlnp

# 4. Test HTTP connectivity to the backend API
curl -s http://localhost:8000/api/cluster/status | python3 -m json.tool

# 5. Trace what happens when you hit the k3s API
curl -v -k https://k3s:6443/version 2>&1 | grep -E '^[<>*]'
# Notice: TLS connection, then HTTP/2, then JSON response

# 6. Find all services and their cluster IPs
kubectl get svc -A -o wide

# 7. Check the Kubernetes DNS config in a pod
kubectl exec deploy/web-app -- cat /etc/resolv.conf
# Should show: nameserver 10.96.0.10 (CoreDNS)

# 8. HTTP status code challenge — what does each return?
for url in \
  'http://localhost:8000/api/lessons' \
  'http://localhost:8000/api/lessons/does-not-exist' \
  'http://localhost:8000/nonexistent'; do
  status=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "$url")
  echo "$status $url"
done
```
